projects.built: Android app bridging the Chamilo e-learning platform and a PDF annotation app already on teachers' tablets: it downloaded student papers from Chamilo, handed them to the annotation app for grading, and uploaded the corrected files back to the platform.

Designed and developed a service component of the train information chain that computes stateful information streams from several sources for several consumers, with performance as a primary constraint.

Designed and developed a secured administration interface to configure and oversee a chain of web applications processing train information for passengers and internal systems; took over as lead developer four months in.
Developed a set of microservices that aggregate files from different sources, persist them, and transcode them for different consumers.

Cross-project technical lead across several web applications selling rail tickets: estimated upcoming functional scope, broke it into user stories with sizing and design, and supported the project teams technically.

Lead developer on a cross-platform Ionic / Angular / Cordova application for Windows (UWP) and iOS that tracks jet engine parts through their cleaning process after teardown, each part identified by an RFID tag scanned with a Bluetooth-connected reader.

Led the group of applications forming SNCF's client referential: replaced its commercial Oracle MDM with a Spring Boot application, cleared technical obsolescence across the platform (Java 8 → 17, Spring 4 → 5, Cloudera 5 → 7), and moved its clusters to a new hosting site.
projects.notable:
The Oracle MDM cost twice: an expensive licence, and a team employed full-time to correct the data it produced. [[Replacing it meant rebuilding a mature product's behaviour with no specification to work from — documentation was absent or years stale, so the incumbent's real rules had to be recovered from the system itself.]]

The house standard was Spring on a dedicated external Tomcat, on ageing on-premise infrastructure. I argued for Spring Boot with embedded Tomcat instead — the better fit, and the furthest the client would go. With a mostly junior team on a critical system, a from-scratch rebuild on a current stack was also the one chance they'd get to learn one.
